![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224989/assets/fd812d1d33801a3ce8368feca0e7d6b87e02bcfab5d904d9b59172d95d0204e5.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224989/assets/e087efb9eb18158005722dd6628cc8f19b22a2b33cad8f67205b8ea398e62c54.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{11}{36}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{6}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{5}{6})}=\frac{6}{5}.
$$
